mappings.note: Cavour's office and two contributions to unifying Italy; LO-3 content asked as a named list, so C-1.1 rather than the analytic reading given to 'explain the process'
the tariff and currency obstacles exist here only to set up what the Zollverein fixed, so this stays on the LO-3 economic-unification family rather than splitting to LO-2 for liberalism

the claim to be supported is that nationalism spreads through a sense of shared belonging - the evolution of the idea itself, LO-3; the cultural means are evidence for the claim, not its subject, so LO-2 stays out
POOR FIT, cited at goal level deliberately. French colonial education in Vietnam is outside this chapter and outside curriculum 103 altogether; no outcome here can be cited without inventing a link
recounts what Sorrieu's first print contains and the vision of nation states behind it; no picture is supplied, so this is the described-from-memory counterpart of the C-1.2 image items
how Romanticism worked on emotion and shared heritage to build national feeling: a cultural movement of the time (LO-2), and the item asks for the mechanism, so no recall competency
the mixed reception of Napoleon's administrative changes - welcomed in Holland and Milan, resented for taxes, censorship and conscription; LO-1 argued rather than listed
the whole process by which Italy was made, from the 1848 failures through the French alliance to Garibaldi's march; LO-3 at its analytic end, unlike the who-was-Cavour item which only wants facts
Britain as a nation built gradually rather than by revolution, argued against the German, Italian and French cases; a comparison, so LO-3 alone

four dissimilarities between the Italian and German unifications - volunteers, secret societies, the role of a chief minister; the textbook never lists these side by side, so the comparison has to be constructed, which keeps C-1.1 out
justifies why the female figure became the nation's allegory, with examples; the allegory content is LO-3 and the demand is argument, the same reading as the other two 'why female figures' items

the thirty-nine states' currencies, weights and tariffs as the commercial classes saw them: the same LO-3 economic-unification material as the Zollverein items. The stored model answer drifts to population growth and slums and does not answer the question asked
five hardships of 1830-48 - population rise, job scarcity, cheap imports, food shortage - the material distress strand of LO-2, asked as a count of reasons so C-1.1
asks the student to choose two countries and explain how nations developed, which is LO-3's whole statement; the choice of cases makes it construction, not recall
five points on Garibaldi's importance to Italian unification; the volunteers and the handover to Victor Emmanuel are LO-3 facts to be listed
Mazzini, Cavour and Garibaldi together in the unification narrative, so Mazzini sits on LO-3 here and not on the LO-2 secret-society side; three known roles described
who Sorrieu was and what his four prints show, recounted without a picture in front of the student; LO-3 for the vision of nation states, C-1.1 for the retrieval
how a nation was visualised, explained through two chosen examples; same allegory content as the four-examples item and the same argued demand
the Club of Thinkers caricature at 3 marks: the student must read the picture and infer that it attacks censorship under the conservative monarchies (LO-2). Genuine source interpretation, hence C-1.2

the whip caricature of Bismarck and the cowed deputies must be described and then interpreted; the content is the autocratic character of the German state that unification produced (LO-3), the demand is source reading
the full formation of the United Kingdom at 5 marks - no prior British nation, the 1707 and 1801 unions, English dominance; a process explained, so LO-3 without C-1.1
the effect of liberalism as an ideology on early nineteenth-century Europe: LO-2, and at 5 marks the political and economic strands must be connected rather than recited
why 1848 earned the name revolution of the liberals - the February abdication, the middle-class risings, the constitutional demands; LO-2 argued at length
examines the claim that 1789 was nationalism's first clear expression, which is the proposition LO-1 rests on; a judgement to be defended, so no recall competency
how economic nationalism fed the wider nationalist sentiment - the thirty-nine currencies, the customs union, the railway network; the Zollverein family on LO-3, here explained as a causal chain
